transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Thank you for being here. As we all know, Riverside Urgent Care Clinic has requested an emergency blood-product reserve that would be stored on-site at their facility and replenished through our hospital blood bank. I'll be making the final decision on whether this reserve can go live and what operating requirements need to accompany it. Currently, Riverside has no blood products assigned to its inventory, so if we approve this, we'd be establishing something entirely new. I'd like to walk through the plan with each of you — transfusion medicine, laboratory operations, courier services, and nursing education — to make sure we've addressed all the critical issues before I finalize anything. Let's start with transfusion medicine: can you walk me through the clinical justification and the proposed product selection for this reserve?

transcript.text: Good morning, Dr. Chen. Thank you for the opportunity to weigh in. From a transfusion medicine perspective, the clinical justification is straightforward: Riverside Urgent Care handles acute presentations — trauma, GI bleeding, obstetric emergencies — where patients may need blood before they can be safely transferred to the main hospital. Having a small on-site reserve bridges that critical gap. As for product selection, I'd like to share an important detail: the transfusion service protocol that was approved for Riverside specifies a starting reserve of exactly 4 O-negative red-cell units and 2 O-positive red-cell units. I reviewed the signed protocol myself. However, I should flag that the inventory request has not yet been entered into our system, so we'll need to make sure that happens before any product is physically moved.
